details:
Beyond Earth: Stories of Equipment Left Behind

Beyond Earth is an interactive educational website inspired by NASA’s Abandoned but Not Forgotten Space Apps Challenge. It introduces young space enthusiasts to the machines and instruments left on the Moon, Mars, and in deep space—and the discoveries they made possible.

How it works

Visitors begin with a narrated 3D guided tour of a virtual space exhibit. They can adjust the tour’s speed and follow captions as they explore.

After the tour, visitors can browse 13 equipment stories organized by destination: the Moon, Mars, and deep space. Each story includes a description, a real NASA photograph, and links to NASA mission and image sources. Visitors can then enter a 3D room, explore an illustrative model, and select its components to highlight them and learn about their roles.

Benefits and intended impact

Space missions are often remembered for their launches and discoveries, while the equipment left behind receives less attention. Beyond Earth aims to make those machines easier to understand and remember.

By combining storytelling, photographs, narration, and interactive models, the project gives students more than one way to explore space history. We hope it encourages curiosity about engineering and science and helps young people see these machines as part of humanity’s continuing exploration of space.

Tools and technology

The website was built with HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. It uses Three.js and WebGL to create the 3D environments and models, and browser speech synthesis for narration. The project uses NASA Space Apps Challenge resources, NASA mission pages, and the NASA Image and Video Library for research and photographs.

The photographs are real NASA imagery, not AI-generated. Some show equipment on Earth before launch, which is noted in their captions. The 3D models are simplified illustrations, not exact replicas.

Creativity and considerations

Beyond Earth presents historical equipment as exhibits in a virtual space museum rather than as a list of facts. Its combination of guided storytelling and selectable 3D components lets visitors learn both the mission story and the purpose of individual parts.

The project also considers accessibility and usability through captions, adjustable narration speed, visual comfort controls on the landing and equipment pages, and desktop and touchscreen navigation. NASA source links are provided so visitors can explore the original information.
